slides: Let's continue with lines and angles: the bisector, the names of angles, and parallel lines.

slides.say: An angle bisector is a line that leaves the vertex of an angle and splits the angle into two equal angles. It goes exactly through the middle. Here's an angle of eighty degrees.

The bisector cuts it in the middle, so we call both halves alpha. Each half is eighty divided by two, forty. If the whole angle is a hundred thirty, each half is sixty-five, and if it's sixty-four, each half is thirty-two.

This is a good moment to talk about names. I marked this angle with alpha. That's a Greek letter, and we often name angles with Greek letters: alpha, beta, gamma, delta. Students sometimes mix up the names, and that's fine, it doesn't really matter.

There's another way to name an angle, with three letters. Put the points B, A and C on the figure. Angle B A C means: start at B, move to A, and continue to C. The letter in the middle, A, is the vertex.
at: start at B, move to A

slides.say: So angle D E F has its vertex at E. And of course, we can also just give the size, like thirty degrees.
Parallel lines are lines whose distance from each other never changes. Here are two lines, a and b.
The distance between two lines is always measured on a line that's perpendicular to both of them. Here it's d, here it's d, and here it's d again. As the lines go on, the distance stays the same.
So parallel lines never meet. They never cross each other, they just go on side by side. We mark them with small arrows.
Now two parallel lines, a and b, and one more line that cuts both of them. We call it a transversal. It makes eight angles, four at each crossing.
The angles with even numbers, two, four, six and eight, are the small angles. All the small angles are equal. Two and four are vertical angles, and six and eight are equal to them too.
The angles with odd numbers, one, three, five and seven, are the large angles. All the large angles are equal too.
And a small angle plus a large angle is always a hundred eighty. Why? Angles one and two sit side by side on line a, so together they make one straight angle.
at: a small angle plus a large angle

slides.say: Let's put numbers on it. At line a, the small angle is sixty degrees, so the large angle next to it is a hundred twenty. And around the crossing, sixty, a hundred twenty, sixty, a hundred twenty.

Now take this whole circle of angles at line a, as if we cut it out, and move it down to line b. It fits exactly. These are the same angles. So all the small ones are sixty, and all the large ones are a hundred twenty.
Another example: if a small angle is fifty-five, every large angle is a hundred eighty minus fifty-five, a hundred twenty-five. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
